messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 27
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: HVAC Technician
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Entrapment: Having no options
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mariana, a 27-year-old HVAC technician, had been working independently for three years, comfortable climbing into tight crawl spaces and navigating the basements of commercial buildings. That comfort ended eighteen months ago, when she was taken during a routine service call to an abandoned warehouse. She had been sent to assess a faulty heating unit in a part of the building that had been sealed off. When she stepped through the door, two men and a woman were waiting. The woman was the one who held her down while the men bound her wrists. Over the next several hours, Mariana was beaten, burned with a cigarette lighter, and repeatedly told she would never leave. The woman whispered to her in Spanish, saying that she had been stupid to come alone, that no one was coming for her. What Mariana remembers most vividly is the feeling of her own helplessness—lying on a concrete floor, her hands raw from the zip ties, the door locked from the outside, every possible exit blocked. She had no options. She could not fight, could not run, could not bargain. She was certain she would die there.

She was eventually freed when a security guard noticed her van still parked after hours, but the event had carved itself into her in ways she did not fully understand until weeks later. At first she could not stop replaying the sound of the door clicking shut. Then the shame arrived—a deep, burning certainty that she had done something to deserve what happened. She had agreed to go alone. She had not checked the work order carefully. She should have known. The memory itself felt wrong, like a movie she had stumbled into, something that could not possibly belong to her. When it surfaced, usually without warning, the emotions hit so hard—terror, shame, a sickening wave of helplessness—that she had to stop whatever she was doing, sit down, and wait until the room stopped spinning.

Work became a minefield. Mariana now found herself flinching every time a female colleague asked to partner on a job. Being alone with a woman in a van or a small mechanical room sent her heart racing; she would make excuses to work separately, even if it meant taking twice as long. She also started to notice injuries everywhere—a scratch on a client's arm, a bruise on her own shin from bumping into a pipe. Each visible wound pulled her back to the smell of her own burnt skin. She could not bear to look. At home, her habits changed. Before bed she checked every window, every door, sometimes three times, then woke at 2 a.m. to do it again, certain that someone had come in while she slept. Any unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a dropped tool—made her jump so violently that a coworker once joked she needed to drink less coffee. Mariana had stopped drinking coffee anyway; caffeine made the startle worse.

She came to believe that she had permanently changed, that the person who had been confident and quick to laugh was gone. She could not trust her own decisions. If she chose a parking spot, she worried it was the wrong one, that someone was watching. If she agreed to a service call in a building she did not know, she spent the whole drive wondering if she was walking into a trap. She began to see danger in everyone, even people who seemed kind. The thought that kept her awake was this: you can never know who will harm you. The woman had seemed ordinary, normal. That was what terrified her most.

What finally brought Mariana to a therapist’s office was a call she almost missed. Her supervisor had assigned her to a job at a women’s shelter, a simple duct repair. She made it to the parking lot, saw the entrance, and could not get out of her van. She sat there for twenty minutes, hands shaking, before driving home and calling in sick. That night she realized she had stopped going to her brother’s house because his girlfriend lived there. She had stopped visiting her own mother, who lived alone but kept a bruise on her arm from a fall. The world had narrowed to her apartment and a few male coworkers she trusted. She was not living. She was hiding. And she was exhausted. When she finally walked into the clinic, she told the intake worker that she wanted to feel safe again, but what she meant was that she wanted to stop being afraid of her own shadow—and she was terrified that she never would.
